scope: Author whole-study qualitative conclusion/limitation prior-art gate only, no per-case tracer/proxy values emitted or comparison computed

authors_prior_art_conclusion_scope: The exploratory analysis suggested that tumor size was positively correlated with both tumor PLOD2 levels and [numeric masked]F-FDG SUVmax. We hypothesize that as sarcomas get larger, they may outstrip their vascular supply, increasing both intra-tumoral hypoxia and aerobic glycolysis. The exploratory analysis also suggested that tumor grade was positively correlated with both [numeric masked]F-FMISO SUVmax, and [numeric masked]F-FMISO T/M SUVmax. Based on this result we hypothesized that higher grade tumors showed increased intra-tumoral hypoxia in our study. A known downstream product of the increased hypoxia is increased PLOD2 levels, which affect collagen fibrin formation [[numeric masked]].

The study has a few limitations. The sample size limits the power of the study to detect associations between in vivo imaging and in vitro tissue measures. However this is an expected challenge given the rarity of patients with soft tissue sarcomas, and the ability to prospectively recruit these patients into trials. Only lesions measuring [numeric masked] cm or greater were included in this study to comply with the registered prospective protocol. Metabolic tumor volume (MTV) and total lesion glycolysis (TLG) are important tumor metrics in determining lesion aggressiveness and differentiation grade. We did not study these metrics because the study protocol stated that we would use the SUVmax and tumor-to-background ratio (TBR) as the outcomes of interest, and post-hoc analysis using these metrics would either inflate the Type I error rate or decrease the power of the study after adjusting for multiple comparisons. Further research is needed to confirm these associations and to investigate the predictive values of MTV and TLG in this setting.

In summary, the small study size limits conclusions about the association of PLOD2 and [numeric masked]F-FMISO uptake levels to support [numeric masked]F-FMISO PET as a companion diagnostic for PLOD2-targeted therapy. Exploratory analyses found positive associations between PLOD2 levels and tumor size, [numeric masked]F-FMISO uptake and tumor grade, and [numeric masked]F-FMISO uptake with [numeric masked]F-FDG uptake. These associations need to be confirmed in a future study in a larger study population.

Tissue microarrays rather than whole sections were used for this study due to the large number of samples. This is a potential limitation of the work as it assesses a smaller area than a whole section and therefore may be more likely to misclassify a hypoxic tumour as normoxic. However, this was assessed in one of the previous studies of CAIX in STS and TMAs were deemed accurate in determining marker expression provided that at least three cores were taken from two separate areas of tumour (Måseide et al, [numeric masked]). Another concern was that there was very limited overlap between expression of the markers in these clinical samples. All three markers are expressed under hypoxia and a degree of coexpression was expected. This may reflect the considerable molecular heterogeneity of STS and indicates that expression of these markers is likely influenced by other pathways. There is therefore a need for a more robust measure of hypoxia in STS than a single protein marker.

Hypoxia-related RNA expression signatures measure changes in multiple genes in response to hypoxia and can account for greater heterogeneity (Harris et al, [numeric masked]). Evaluation of a biomarker at the RNA level also reduces inconsistencies in methodology and interpretation between laboratories compared with IHC and is more likely to be reproducible in clinical practice. Hypoxia RNA expression signatures have made the most progress towards use as predictive biomarkers for hypoxia targeted therapy in the clinic, with two signatures (Toustrup et al, [numeric masked]; Eustace et al, [numeric masked]) currently undergoing prospective validation in phase III trials in head and neck cancer. Recently, one of these signatures has demonstrated prognostic value in a cohort of STS patients (Aggerholm-Pedersen et al, [numeric masked]). However, hypoxia signatures generally perform best in the tumour types they were developed for (Eustace et al, [numeric masked]) and the signature genes correlated poorly with oxygen electrode measurements in [numeric masked] patients indicating that it may not be a good measure of hypoxia in STS (Aggerholm-Pedersen et al, [numeric masked]). It may be more appropriate to derive a hypoxia signature specific to STS, as it must be a robust measure of hypoxia if it is to be used as a predictive biomarker for hypoxia targeted therapy. The other tissue available in the VorteX-Biobank is intended to be used for this purpose with the eventual aim of a biomarker-driven trial of hypoxia targeted adjuvant/neoadjuvant therapy in STS.

In summary, evaluation of protein hypoxia markers in a modern phase III clinical trial cohort suggests that CAIX is the best current known hypoxia marker. A simple binary scoring system can easily be implemented to define positivity but still requires manual pathology assessment. However, other measures of hypoxia such as gene signatures may perform better and be more reflective of hypoxia across different subtypes, compensating for greater heterogeneity. Further work is needed to develop a gene signature and confirm that it is a true measure of hypoxia by comparing this to CAIX and other methods of assessing hypoxia (e.g. imaging/electrodes) before this could be taken forward as a prognostic or predictive biomarker for clinical trials.
